object_types.name: Employee
object_types.definition: A person who is employed; identified the same way as a Person.

source_references.excerpt: Employees are persons; every employee is also a person, identified the same way.
A manager is an employee with extra responsibilities.

object_types.name: Department
object_types.definition: An organizational unit that employs persons and may be managed by a manager.

source_references.excerpt: Each department has a department code.

source_references.excerpt: Each department has a department code.

object_types.name: DepartmentName
object_types.definition: The name of a department, e.g. Payroll or Field Operations.

source_references.excerpt: Departments also each have a department name, like "Payroll" or "Field Operations", and no two share a name.

ambiguities.description: Managers manage 'at most one department', and 'some managers... manage none' -- confirming this role is optional (not mandatory) for Manager. Is it truly optional, or could there be an intended rule that some managers must manage a department (e.g. senior managers)? Currently modeled as optional based on explicit statement.

source_references.excerpt: A manager manages at most one department. Some managers are between assignments and manage none.

ambiguities.description: Is there a constraint that only Managers (not regular Employees) can manage a Department, and is the reverse -- that a Department can only be managed by a Manager who also works in that same department, or could a Manager manage a different department than the one they work in? The transcript does not clarify whether Manager.manages Department must equal or relate to Employee.works_in Department for that manager.

source_references.excerpt: Every employee works in exactly one department.
A manager manages at most one department.

ambiguities.description: The subtype chain Person -> Employee -> Manager all share the same reference_mode 'person_id' since they are identified the same way; however, since Manager and Employee are entity types with reference_mode duplicated from Person, is it necessary to model separate identifier fact types for each subtype, or should identification be inherited directly without redundant fact types? This is a modeling convention question rather than a business ambiguity, but worth flagging for implementation clarity.

ambiguities.description: Is a Department required to have a Manager? The transcript states managers manage at most one department and some manage none, but does not state whether every Department must have exactly one Manager or can be unmanaged. This affects the mandatory/optional status of the Department role in 'Manager manages Department'.
